A black squall front is coming up behind the towers and every blade in the picture is dropping to the straight-down safe position at the same moment — the near ones already down, the middle ones still falling, the far ones only just starting to move.
Twenty pigeons are sitting shoulder to shoulder along the nearest cable and one of them is lifting off it, wings wide open, the whole cable still bouncing in a long slow wave where it left.
Blue-white sparks are jumping off the rim of a cable drum in a hard spray and dying out in the cold air, throwing their flicker up onto the underside of the timber above them.
Ice a finger thick sheathes every cable and is letting go in long clear shards, a whole run of them dropping away into the fog below while the freed wire whips and sheds white dust.
A cat is lying flat out asleep in the warm updraught of a roof vent right beside the iron anchor ring, one paw over its eyes, the steam combing past it and not disturbing it at all.
Snow has built along the top of every cable in a thin white ridge and the wind is lifting it off in a long smoking veil that drifts sideways across the tower.
A paper kite with a rag tail has wound itself round a blade and is tugging and snapping up there, its string running away taut out of the frame.
Rain is coming across in a hard slant and every cable is shedding water off its underside in an unbroken curtain of drips, the leads below running like a stream.
A crow has landed on the very top of the tower and is working at the halyard knot with its beak, while fifteen more crows sit along the cables behind it waiting.
The wind has the whole fan of cables humming and visibly shivering, and a loose halyard end is beating and cracking against the ironwork.
A moth cloud has found the lit lamp and is boiling round it, hundreds of pale moths thick in the light, their shadows crossing and crossing the painted timber.
Steam from a roof vent has risen straight up into the cables and is being shredded by them into long flat ribbons that lean away downwind.
A gull has carried a whole herring up onto the tower gallery and is standing on it with both feet while three more gulls come in low and fast over the slates.
A counterweight has run away from its brake and is swinging in a long slow arc under its bracket, the chain slapping the lattice at each end of the swing, the blades above moving with it.
A chimney has just caught fire and is throwing a fountain of orange sparks up through the cables, and the sparks are going out one by one as they clear the wires.
Several hundred starlings are pouring along just above the cables in one dense flowing ribbon and shearing sideways round the near tower without touching it.
Hail is bouncing off the slates in a white spatter, rattling loudly on the tower's painted timber, and collecting in the gutter in a pale drift.
A cable has parted at its turnbuckle and lies whipping loose across the leads, its cut end bright and fraying, the slack still running out of it.
Two dozen bats are hunting the moths round the lit lantern room, cutting in and out of its coloured light and flickering black against the panes.
The frost is letting go of the ironwork in patches, sheets of rime sliding off the gallery rail and shattering on the leads below in bright dust.
A whole loft of pigeons, thirty birds, has just been let out and is going round the near tower in one tight ring, the ring tilting as it turns.
The smoke of forty chimneys is leaning all one way across the picture and the cables are cutting flat black bands straight through it.
A rooftop safety valve has gone off right beside the tower's foot and a jet of white steam is climbing hard through the blades, hiding one of them completely.
A fox is trotting along the roof ridge behind the tower as if this were an ordinary road, and has stopped with one paw up to look at a pigeon.
The wind has got under a stack of spare paddles and knocked them over, and they are sliding one after another down the wet slates toward the gutter.
